legal: Independent research from public sources and the Sayari knowledge graph. It is not legal advice. Sayari risk flags are graph-level indicators derived from records and networks; they are not findings of wrongdoing by any named company. Sayari-flagged suppliers that appear here have not been shown to supply tungsten to ITER or Commonwealth Fusion Systems unless a link says so.

overview.headline: Tungsten from mine to fusion reactor, and where the human-rights risk sits
overview.summary: Every magnetic-confinement fusion design puts tungsten where the plasma hits hardest: ITER's divertor alone holds about 300,000 tungsten monoblocks [S08], and ITER replaced its beryllium first wall with tungsten in 2023 [S07]. China mines 79% of the world's tungsten [S01]. The rest comes partly from conflict-affected places: eastern DRC, the Rwanda transit corridor, and armed-group territory in Myanmar [S17, S22]. This project traces that chain with Tavily web research and Sayari's corporate and trade graph, then proposes two fixes for fusion procurement.
overview.caveat: Sayari shows no tungsten shipments into ITER or Commonwealth Fusion Systems. The links from mines to fusion buyers on this site are sector-level routes and named-supplier records; none of them shows that tungsten from a specific abusive mine reached a reactor.

materials.component: Divertor armour, about 300,000 monoblocks in ITER [S08]. ITER first-wall armour since 2023 [S07]. Future burning-plasma designs plan to use it [S07].
materials.producers: China 67,000 t; Vietnam 3,000; Kazakhstan 2,400; Russia 2,000; N. Korea 2,000; Bolivia 1,700; Rwanda 1,300 (2025) [S01].
materials.risks: DRC forced and child labor on the US DOL list [S15]. Rwanda as a transit point for laundered Congolese 3T minerals [S17, S19]. Armed-group mining in Myanmar [S22]. Chinese export controls [S25]. Defined as a conflict mineral in US and EU law [S26, S27].

materials.component: First-wall armour (dropped by ITER in 2023) and neutron multiplier in breeding blankets [S07, S10, S11].
materials.producers: USA 230 t; Brazil 80; China 77; Nigeria 40 (2025) [S02]. Materion's Spor Mountain, Utah, is the largest producer [S46].
materials.risks: Chronic beryllium disease among workers; OSHA cut the exposure limit tenfold [S45]. Xinjiang Nonferrous, which mines beryllium, was added to the UFLPA Entity List in 2024 [S23]. No artisanal beryl abuse evidence specific to beryllium was found.

materials.component: Breeding blanket (PbLi, FLiBe or ceramic). Needs Li-6 enrichment to breed tritium [S11].
materials.producers: Australia 92,000 t; China 62,000; Chile 56,000; Zimbabwe 28,000; Argentina 23,000 (2025) [S03]. Li-6 enrichment only in Russia and China [S38].
materials.risks: Indigenous water rights in the Atacama [S35, S34, S36]. Evictions and child labor at Zimbabwe mines [S37]. Mercury legacy of COLEX enrichment [S39]. SDIC Xinjiang Lithium on the UFLPA list (2026) [S24].

materials.component: Low-temperature superconducting magnets, as used in ITER.
materials.producers: Niobium: Brazil 104,000 t of 112,000 (2025) [S04]; CBMM supplies over 80% [S43]. Tin: China 71,000; Indonesia 61,000; Peru 33,000; DRC 27,000; Myanmar 12,000 [S05].
materials.risks: Tin is a 3TG conflict mineral. Forced and child labor in DRC tin [S15]. Child labor in Bolivian tin [S16]. Deaths at illegal tin mines in Bangka-Belitung, Indonesia [S44]. Niobium: no rights evidence found.

materials.component: High-temperature superconducting magnet tape for CFS and Tokamak Energy [S12]. CFS ordered more than 10,000 km of tape from Fujikura [S13].
materials.producers: China produced most yttrium, Burma a significant share; 70% of US imports come from China [S06].
materials.risks: Heavy rare earths from Myanmar's Kachin State: $1.4bn trade, militia control and toxic pollution [S40, S41]. Chinese export licensing on yttrium and gadolinium since April 2025 [S42].

recommendation.text: Tungsten has the strongest combination of a traceable supply chain and documented human-rights evidence, so this project traces it.
reasons: It is a legally defined conflict mineral. Dodd-Frank §1502 and SEC Rule 13p-1 cover wolframite and tungsten [S26], and EU Regulation 2017/821 imposes importer due diligence [S27].

The supply chain has choke points. There are about 57 tungsten smelters, each with a public RMI ID and audit status [S28, S29]. Ores (HS 2611), tungstates (2841) and metal (8101) appear as their own lines in trade data, which is what made the Sayari trace possible [X19].
The abuse evidence spans several regions: DRC forced and child labor [S15], Rwanda laundering [S17], and conflict areas in Myanmar [S22].
recommendation.runnerup: Lithium and REBCO rare earths have strong abuse evidence [S37, S40], but fusion-grade Li-6 comes only from Russia and China [S38], and yttrium has no dedicated US trade code [S06]. Both are close to untraceable today. Beryllium is dominated by one regulated US producer [S46], and niobium by one Brazilian company [S43].

brief.from: Fusion Tungsten Tier Map (independent OSINT research)
brief.re: Human-rights due diligence for tungsten in fusion procurement
brief.title: Fusion buyers cannot see where their tungsten comes from. Two fixes.
brief.bottom: Tungsten is the material fusion cannot do without, and the one with the best tools for tracing it. Yet neither ITER nor Commonwealth Fusion Systems shows up as a tungsten buyer in Sayari's trade data [X01, X02]. Public funders should require a tier map and a smelter audit check before awarding tungsten-bearing contracts, and should extend existing conflict-minerals reporting to fusion supply contracts.

problem.t: China mines 79% of the world's tungsten and has licensed exports since February 2025 [S01, S25].
The DRC tungsten trade involves forced and child labor, and Congolese 3T minerals are laundered through Rwanda [S15, S17, S19]. Rwanda now supplies up to 20% of US primary concentrate [S20].
Myanmar ore from armed-group areas reaches Chinese smelters in growing volumes [S22].
Only 34 of 57 tungsten smelters were RMAP-conformant in May 2024 [S29], and audited smelters have passed while sourcing from M23-held areas (for coltan) [S31].
Sayari shows no inbound tungsten for ITER or CFS. The visible links stop at component makers such as Plansee, which buys tungsten wire from a Xiamen Tungsten subsidiary [X01, X02, X05].
Fusion's tungsten demand is small next to tooling and defense. But every publicly funded fusion contract is a point of leverage that no other buyer of the same tungsten has.

tech.name: A tier map and smelter check as a procurement gate
tech.what: Any ITER, F4E or DOE contract that delivers tungsten parts above a set threshold must include a tier map from mine to component, built with a trade and registry graph such as Sayari. Every smelter named in it must be checked against the RMI conformant list before award and at each delivery.

how.t: The data exists today. Sayari resolved Plansee, Xiamen Tungsten, H.C. Starck, Masan, Nui Phao and Trinity Nyakabingo, and linked them through HS 2611, 2841 and 8101 records [X03, X05, X07, X08, X10, X11].
Smelters carry RMI IDs, and the RMI publishes a tungsten conformant list [S28, S33].

Bidders submit a machine-readable bill of materials: smelter RMI ID, mine of origin, HS codes and shipment record IDs. An automated screen flags sanctions, UFLPA, ILAB and conflict-mineral risk factors, as Sayari already labels them.
A flag does not disqualify a bidder. It triggers enhanced due diligence and a documented response, in line with the OECD five-step framework that both US and EU regimes reference.

Sanctions screening comes as a by-product. Sayari already shows ITER and CFS records of tungsten exports to Russian recipients, one of them sanctioned [X01, X02, X16], which procurement teams should verify.

policy.name: Extend conflict-minerals reporting to fusion supply contracts
policy.what: Dodd-Frank §1502 reaches only SEC-listed manufacturers [S26], and EU 2017/821 only importers of ores and metals [S27]. Most fusion developers are private, and most of their tungsten arrives as finished parts, so neither regime covers it. Fix that gap through contract terms and grant conditions.

how.t: DOE adds a clause to fusion awards (for example, milestone-based development agreements and ITER in-kind procurement) requiring an annual conflict-minerals report modelled on Form SD for tungsten, tin and tantalum content.
The EU applies the same expectation to F4E contracts, building on its 2025 recognition of RMAP as an equivalent scheme [S30].
Both treat DRC, Rwanda and Myanmar origins as red flags requiring on-the-ground checks, not just paper audits, given the 2024 loss of ITSCI's RMI recognition [S32].
The legal definitions already exist: 'wolframite and its derivative tungsten' [S26] and 'tin, tantalum and tungsten, their ores, and gold' [S27].

objections.t: Cost and burden: tier mapping costs little next to a divertor contract, and suppliers such as A.L.M.T. and H.C. Starck already report to RMAP [S33].
Supply squeeze: with China licensing exports [S25], buyers will be tempted to accept any non-Chinese ore. That is the reason checks on DRC, Rwanda and Myanmar origins matter more now, not less.
Data gaps: customs data rarely names the consignee for finished components, which is why ITER and CFS are invisible [X01, X02]. The gate makes suppliers supply that data.

next: ITER and DOE pilot the gate on one tungsten work package, using RMI's tungsten list [S28].
Pull and verify the Sayari source records for ITER's and CFS's HS 810199 exports to Russia [X01, X02].
Ask Plansee, A.L.M.T. and H.C. Starck for their RMAP smelter IDs and mine-of-origin lists for fusion orders [S33].
Publish an annual fusion-sector tungsten sourcing summary.
facts: 79% of 2025 tungsten mine output came from China [S01].
DRC tungsten is on the DOL list for forced and child labor [S15].
The UN identifies Rwanda as a transit point for Congolese 3T minerals [S19].
Myanmar ore to China rose 97% in early 2026 [S22].
Xiamen Honglu shipped HS 810196 tungsten wire to Plansee India in 2026 [X05].
No inbound tungsten for ITER or CFS appears in Sayari [X01, X02].
inferences: That DRC laundering patterns documented for coltan also apply to wolframite.
That Bolivian cooperative child labor extends to tungsten.
That a procurement gate would change supplier behaviour at fusion's small volumes.
That Plansee's Indian imports feed parts for fusion customers. This is not shown.

tools.use: Entity resolution, upstream supply-chain tracing, trade search by HS code and country, watchlist screening to depth 2, and risk-factor definitions [X19].

tools.name: This site
tools.use: A static site with D3 and topojson, adapted from the Lindt Cocoa Tier Map; all content lives in data/*.json.

steps: Listed the raw materials each fusion subsystem needs and compared production concentration and rights evidence across five materials.
Chose tungsten for its legal conflict-mineral status, its smelter audit list and its distinct HS codes.
Resolved the deployment buyers (ITER, CFS), the component maker (Plansee) and the mining and processing anchors in Sayari, then verified the IDs.
Pulled upstream supply chains filtered by HS 2611, 8101, 2841 and 2849, and ran supplier and buyer searches for six origin countries.
Screened each anchor with Sayari's watchlist and recorded every risk flag, separating direct flags from possible-match (psa_) flags.
Cross-checked Sayari links against public sources and labelled each claim with a confidence level.
Rated the five risks for severity and traceability, then wrote the brief, separating verified facts from inferences.
confidence: A primary or official source states it: USGS, UN, DOL, a regulator, or the company itself.
A credible NGO, academic or press source reports it.
A record in the Sayari graph shows it. It has not been checked against the underlying document.
Analyst judgment or an illustrative link with no direct source.
ratings: Severity (1–5) weighs how grave the documented harm is (violence, forced or child labor), how widespread it is, and how strong the evidence is.
Traceability (1–5) rates how far a fusion buyer could follow tungsten from the risk back to a named mine, using trade data, registries, smelter audits and Sayari.
Both ratings are judgments made by this project, not scores taken from Sayari.

limits: Sayari's shipper_name and receiver_name filters were ignored, so counterparty searches used the company name as free text with an HS code. Some facet queries timed out (HTTP 408).
Trade counts are shipment rows, not tonnes or dollars. Compact results do not include volumes.
EU and US customs data rarely name the consignee for finished components, which is the likely reason ITER and CFS are invisible as tungsten buyers.
Russian import records can name a brand owner or manufacturer as the shipper. The ITER→NIIEFA and CFS→S-Innovatsii rows need source-record verification.
psa_ flags rest on 'possibly the same as' entity matches. Subtier forced-labor flags come from network analysis, not findings against the company.
Several companies appear under duplicate Sayari records (Plansee, Xiamen Honglu, Trinity Nyakabingo); they were not merged.
Sayari entity links require a Sayari login.
Five sources link to the publisher's site rather than the exact article, because the article URL was not captured [S13, S37, S42, S46, S47].
